More than a billion years ago, in a galaxy we will never see, two black holes began their final dance.
Each was about thirty times heavier than our Sun.
In a fraction of a second, they became one. And three Suns' worth of mass vanished, into pure ripples in spacetime.
For that one moment, it released more power than every star in the observable universe, combined.
The ripples travelled outward at the speed of light, crossing the dark for more than a billion years,
until, on September fourteenth, twenty fifteen, they washed quietly over a small blue world.
And we were listening. Lie-go: two beams of laser light, in tunnels four kilometres long.
As the wave passed, it stretched one arm, and squeezed the other,
by one thousandth the width of a proton.
It is like measuring the distance to the nearest star, to within the width of a human hair.
The whole signal lasted two tenths of a second.
Einstein predicted these waves in nineteen sixteen. A century later, for the first time, we felt the universe tremble.
